meta.title: The Sealed Tomb of the Capulets
meta.unit: Romeo and Juliet — Shakespeare's language, characters and plot
meta.subject: English: Language & Literature
meta.author: ISH English

story.introTitle: A torch in the Capulet vault
story.intro: The iron gate of the Capulet tomb has clanged shut behind you, and your torch is burning low. Friar Laurence carved a way out into the cold stone, but only a true reader of the play can follow it. Solve each clue along the wall to lift the final lock before the watchmen arrive.
story.outro: The last lock springs and the heavy door grinds open onto torchlit Verona. You traced the lovers' language, their voices and their tragic story, and read your way out of the tomb. Like the Prince at the play's close, you leave knowing the whole sad tale.

stations.name: The Cipher on the Crypt Door
stations.narrative: Two words are chiselled into the crypt door in a simple shifted code. Decode them to name what dooms the lovers from the very start.

content.prompt: Shift every letter back to read the two words the Prologue uses to describe the lovers.

hints: Every letter has been pushed forward through the alphabet by the same small step.
Shift each letter back by 4 (so W becomes S, and X becomes T).
The Prologue calls the lovers 'a pair of ____ ____ lovers' — it means fated by the stars.
stations.reveal: Correct — STAR-CROSSED. In the Prologue Shakespeare calls Romeo and Juliet 'a pair of star-crossed lovers', telling us from the first lines that fate is against them.

stations.name: Juliet's Balcony Line
stations.narrative: Below a carved balcony, a single word has worn away from one of the play's most famous lines. Restore it to release the catch.

content.text: On her balcony, Juliet sighs, 'O ____, ____, wherefore art thou ____?' — asking why the boy she loves must be a Montague.

hints: Juliet is speaking about the young man she has just fallen in love with at the feast.
'Wherefore' means 'why', not 'where' — she is asking why he must be a Montague.
His name begins with 'R'; the whole line is 'wherefore art thou Romeo?'
stations.reveal: ROMEO. 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' means 'why are you Romeo?' — Juliet wishes he were not a Montague, the enemy of her family, the Capulets.

stations.name: The Voice on the Plaque
stations.narrative: A brass plaque records a witty, biting line spoken just after the speaker is given a fatal wound. Name who says it.

content.quote: Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man.

hints: This speaker is Romeo's quick-witted friend, famous for jokes and the 'Queen Mab' speech.
Even while dying from Tybalt's sword, he cannot resist a pun — 'a grave man' means both serious and dead.
His name begins with 'M' and his death turns the play from comedy toward tragedy.
stations.reveal: MERCUTIO. Even as he dies of Tybalt's wound he puns — 'a grave man' means both 'serious' and 'in a grave'. His death is the turning point that drives Romeo to revenge.

stations.name: The Order of the Tragedy
stations.narrative: Four carved tiles show key moments of the story, jumbled out of order. Lay them in the order they happen to free the next bolt.

content.prompt: Put these events from the play in the order they happen.
items: Romeo and Juliet meet and fall in love at the Capulet feast
Friar Laurence secretly marries Romeo and Juliet
Romeo is banished from Verona for killing Tybalt
Romeo and Juliet die in the Capulet tomb

stations.answer: Romeo and Juliet meet and fall in love at the Capulet feast|Friar Laurence secretly marries Romeo and Juliet|Romeo is banished from Verona for killing Tybalt|Romeo and Juliet die in the Capulet tomb
acceptedAnswers: Romeo and Juliet meet and fall in love at the Capulet feast|Friar Laurence secretly marries Romeo and Juliet|Romeo is banished from Verona for killing Tybalt|Romeo and Juliet die in the Capulet tomb
hints: Start with the night the lovers first meet — everything else follows from it.
The secret wedding comes before the street fight in which Tybalt dies.
Meet, marry, banishment, then the deaths in the tomb.
stations.reveal: Right order — they meet, marry in secret, Romeo is banished after killing Tybalt, and the play ends with both lovers dead in the tomb. Shakespeare drives us swiftly from joy to disaster in only a few days.

stations.name: The Final Lock
stations.narrative: One word, spelled exactly right, lifts the last lock. It names the kind of speech in which a character, alone on stage, reveals their private thoughts aloud.

content.definition: A speech in which a character, alone on stage, speaks their inner thoughts aloud to the audience — like Juliet's 'Gallop apace' speech as she waits for Romeo.

hints: It is the technical term for a character thinking aloud, alone, so the audience hears their true feelings.
Nine letters, beginning with 'soli-' (from the Latin for 'alone').
stations.reveal: SOLILOQUY — a speech delivered alone on stage that lets the audience hear a character's private thoughts. Shakespeare uses soliloquies to reveal Romeo's and Juliet's deepest feelings. The last lock lifts — you are free.
